problems.title: Find Two Numbers That Add to a Target
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer target, return the indices of two distinct elements whose sum equals target. Exactly one valid pair exists, and the same index cannot be used twice.
problems.approach: Hash map of previously seen numbers
steps: Create a HashMap from number to its index.
Scan the array from left to right. For each number x, compute complement = target - x.
If the complement is already in the map, return its stored index and the current index.
Otherwise record x and its index, then continue. Store only after checking to avoid using the current element twice.
problems.interviewTip: Explain why you check for the complement before inserting the current element. HashMap operations are O(1) on average.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation

problems.title: Check Whether Brackets Are Balanced
problems.statement: Given a string containing only parentheses (), square brackets [], and curly braces {}, determine whether every opening bracket is closed by the correct type in the correct order.

example.explanation: Every closing bracket matches the most recently opened unmatched bracket.

steps: Create an empty stack of characters.
For an opening bracket, push its matching closing bracket onto the stack.
For a closing bracket, the stack must be nonempty and its top must equal that character; otherwise return false.
After the entire string, return true only if the stack is empty.
problems.interviewTip: Mention why a counter cannot handle mixed bracket types or nesting order.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of a Contiguous Subarray
problems.statement: Given a nonempty array of integers, find the greatest possible sum among all contiguous, nonempty subarrays. Negative numbers are allowed.
steps: Initialize currentSum and bestSum to the first element, which handles all-negative arrays.
For each subsequent element x, decide whether to start a new subarray at x or extend the previous one: currentSum = max(x, currentSum + x).
Update bestSum = max(bestSum, currentSum).
Return bestSum after processing every element.
problems.interviewTip: Be ready to explain why initializing to zero would give the wrong answer for an all-negative input.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeated Characters
problems.statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest contiguous substring with no repeated character. Treat Java characters as UTF-16 code units for this problem.

example.explanation: The substring "abc" has three distinct characters; any longer window repeats a character.

constraints: s may contain letters, digits, symbols or spaces.
steps: Start a window at left = 0 and maintain a map from character to its latest index.
Move right across the string. If the current character was seen within the current window, move left just past its previous index.
Update the character's latest index to right.
Update best with the window length right - left + 1; return best after the scan.
problems.interviewTip: Why use max when moving left? A previously seen character may be outside the current window.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation

Continue shrinking past duplicates; best remains 3

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays into One
problems.statement: Given two integer arrays sorted in nondecreasing order, return a new sorted array containing every element from both arrays, including duplicates.

example.explanation: Compare the front elements and append the smaller one. Both occurrences of 3 are retained.

constraints: Both input arrays are sorted in nondecreasing order.
problems.approach: Walk both sorted arrays with two indices
steps: Create a result array of length a.length + b.length, and start pointers i and j at zero.
While both pointers are in range, compare a[i] and b[j]. Copy the smaller value into the next result position and advance its pointer.
After one array is exhausted, copy all remaining values from the other array.
Return the result. Empty inputs and duplicates work without special handling.
problems.interviewTip: Explain the loop invariant: the result prefix is always sorted and contains the smallest elements processed so far.

problems.title: Find the First Position of a Target
problems.statement: Given a sorted integer array that may contain duplicates and a target integer, return the index of its first occurrence. Return -1 if it does not occur.

example.explanation: The target appears at indices 1, 2, and 3, so the first position is 1.

constraints: nums is sorted in nondecreasing order.
steps: Set left to 0 and right to nums.length, representing a half-open search interval.
While left is smaller than right, compute mid without adding left and right directly.
If nums[mid] is smaller than target, discard the left half including mid; otherwise keep mid and the left half.
When the interval closes, left is the first index whose value is at least target. Return it only if it is in range and equals target; otherwise return -1.
problems.interviewTip: Ordinary binary search finds any match; the lower-bound variation deliberately continues searching left for duplicates.

problems.title: List Binary Tree Values Level by Level
problems.statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return a list of levels from top to bottom. Within each level, values must appear from left to right. Return an empty list for an empty tree.

example.explanation: Visit the root first, then its two children, then the next level's children in left-to-right order.

steps: Return an empty result if root is null; otherwise put root into a queue.
At the start of each level, save the queue size. Exactly that many nodes belong to the current level.
Remove each of those nodes, append its value to the current level, and enqueue its non-null left and right children in that order.
Append the completed level to the result, then repeat until the queue is empty.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n) including the output and BFS queue
problems.interviewTip: The saved queue size separates levels. Without it, newly enqueued children would be mixed into their parent's level.

problems.title: Minimum Coins Needed for an Amount
problems.statement: Given distinct positive coin denominations and a nonnegative amount, find the minimum number of coins needed to make exactly that amount. Each denomination can be used any number of times. Return -1 if no combination exists.

example.explanation: Two coins of value 3 make 6. Taking 4 then two 1s would require three coins.

steps: Let dp[x] mean the minimum number of coins needed for amount x. Set dp[0] to zero and every other entry to an unreachable sentinel amount + 1.
For each amount x from 1 to the target, try every coin whose value is at most x.
If dp[x - coin] is reachable, consider dp[x - coin] + 1 and keep the smallest candidate for dp[x].
Return dp[amount] if it is reachable, otherwise -1. The zero-amount case correctly returns zero.
problems.interviewTip: Explain why choosing the largest available coin greedily can fail: for [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, greedy uses 4+1+1, while optimal uses 3+3.
dryRun: dp[3]=1 via coin 3, dp[4]=1 via coin 4

variants.name: Top-down memoized recursion
variants.explanation: Compute minCoins(x) from minCoins(x-coin), cache each amount; same asymptotic work but recursive.

variants.name: Bottom-up dynamic programming over amounts
variants.explanation: Let dp[x] mean the minimum number of coins needed for amount x. Set dp[0] to zero and every other entry to an unreachable sentinel amount + 1. For each amount x from 1 to the target, try every coin whose value is at most x. If dp[x - coin] is reachable, consider dp[x - coin] + 1 and keep the smallest candidate for dp[x]. Return dp[amount] if it is reachable, otherwise -1. The zero-amount case correctly returns zero.

problems.title: Reverse a Singly Linked List
problems.statement: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the links in place and return the new head. Return null for an empty list.

example.explanation: Every next pointer is redirected toward the previous node; node 4 becomes the head.

problems.approach: Iterative pointer reversal with three references
steps: Initialize prev to null and curr to the head. The reversed portion is initially empty.
Save curr.next in next before modifying the current node.
Point curr.next to prev, then advance prev to curr and curr to next.
Repeat until curr is null. Return prev, which now points to the new head. An empty list returns null.
problems.interviewTip: Draw the three pointers and explain why saving next before changing curr.next prevents losing the remaining list.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation

variants.explanation: Store every value and write them back in reverse. Changes node values, unlike true pointer reversal.

problems.title: Find the Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree
problems.statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth, defined as the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. An empty tree has depth zero.

example.explanation: The longest root-to-leaf paths are 3 → 20 → 15 and 3 → 20 → 7, each containing three nodes.

problems.approach: Iterative depth-first traversal with an explicit stack
steps: If root is null, return zero immediately.
Push the root with depth one onto a stack.
Pop a node and its depth, update the maximum, then push each non-null child with depth plus one.
Continue until the stack is empty and return the maximum. Using an explicit stack avoids recursion-stack overflow for very deep trees.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n) worst case for the explicit stack
problems.interviewTip: Contrast DFS with BFS and mention that a skewed tree can be 10,000 nodes deep, so iterative traversal is safer than recursion in Java.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation
dryRun: 9 is leaf depth 2, children 15 and 7 under 20 have depth 3

variants.name: Recursive depth
variants.explanation: Depth = 1 + max(leftDepth,rightDepth), and null depth = 0.

variants.name: Iterative depth-first traversal with an explicit stack
variants.spaceComplexity: O(n) worst case for the explicit stack
variants.explanation: If root is null, return zero immediately. Push the root with depth one onto a stack. Pop a node and its depth, update the maximum, then push each non-null child with depth plus one. Continue until the stack is empty and return the maximum. problems.title: Merge Overlapping Time Intervals
problems.statement: Given an array of closed integer intervals [start, end], merge intervals that overlap or share an endpoint. Return the disjoint merged intervals sorted by start time.

example.explanation: The first two intervals overlap, and [8,10] shares endpoint 10 with [10,12].

constraints: Each interval has exactly two integers start and end
problems.approach: Sort by starting point, then sweep and merge
steps: Return an empty two-dimensional array if there are no intervals.
Sort intervals by start using Integer.compare to avoid overflow.
Keep a current merged interval. If the next start is at most the current end, extend the end to the larger of the two ends.
Otherwise append the current interval to the answer and begin a new one. Append the final interval and return the result.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n) scanning
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the output; sorting may use additional implementation-dependent memory
problems.interviewTip: Ask whether intervals are closed: if touching endpoints count as overlap, use nextStart <= currentEnd, not <.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation

problems.title: Find the K Most Frequent Numbers
problems.statement: Given a nonempty integer array nums and integer k, return the k distinct numbers with the highest frequencies. If frequencies tie, prefer the smaller number. Return the selected numbers ordered by descending frequency, then ascending numeric value.

example.explanation: 2 occurs three times. Both 1 and 4 occur twice, so the smaller value 1 wins the tie.

problems.approach: Frequency map and size-k min-heap of the worst retained candidate
steps: Count occurrences of each number in a HashMap.
Maintain a min-heap whose root is the worst selected candidate: lower frequency is worse; for equal frequencies, larger numeric value is worse.
Offer each distinct number to the heap. When the heap exceeds k entries, remove its root.
Extract the k retained numbers, then sort them by descending frequency and ascending value to meet the output ordering.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n + u log k + k log k), where u is the number of distinct values
problems.interviewTip: Explain the min-heap ordering carefully: on ties, the larger value must be removed first so the smaller value remains.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation
dryRun: Tie between 1 and 4 (2 each); smaller 1 ranks first

variants.explanation: Sort distinct values by descending frequency and ascending number for ties.

problems.title: Find the Number That Appears Once
problems.statement: An integer array contains exactly one value that appears once; every other value appears exactly twice. Return the value that appears once without using extra collections.

example.explanation: The repeated values cancel in XOR, leaving -2.

constraints: Exactly one value occurs once; all others occur twice.
problems.approach: Use XOR to cancel equal pairs
steps: Start an accumulator at zero.
XOR each array value into the accumulator. XOR of identical numbers is zero, and XOR with zero leaves a number unchanged.
Because XOR is associative and commutative, every duplicate pair cancels regardless of order.
Return the accumulator, which is the single unpaired number.
problems.interviewTip: Demonstrate x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. This works for negative integers too.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation

problems.title: Find the First Non-Repeating Character
problems.statement: Given a string containing only lowercase English letters, return the zero-based index of its first character that occurs exactly once in the entire string. Return -1 if every character repeats.

example.explanation: The character 'w' at index 1 occurs once, and every earlier character repeats.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters a through z.
problems.approach: Two passes with a fixed-size frequency array
steps: Create an integer array of 26 zeros, one counter for each lowercase letter.
Scan the string once, increasing the count for each character.
Scan the string again from left to right, returning the first index whose character has frequency one.
If no such character exists, return -1. An empty string also returns -1.
problems.interviewTip: Counting alone is not enough: the second pass preserves the original order and identifies the first unique character.

problems.title: Search in a Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement: An ascending array of distinct integers was rotated at an unknown pivot. Given a target, return its index, or -1 if absent. Aim for logarithmic time.

example.explanation: The target 3 is at index 4. One side of each search interval remains sorted.

constraints: All array elements are distinct integers.
problems.approach: Binary search while identifying the sorted half
steps: Initialize left at zero and right at the last index.
While left is not past right, find the middle index and return it if the middle element equals target.
If nums[left] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted. Keep it when target lies between nums[left] inclusive and nums[mid] exclusive; otherwise search right.
Otherwise the right half is sorted. Keep it when target is greater than nums[mid] and at most nums[right]; otherwise search left.
Each iteration discards at least half of the remaining range. Return -1 if no match is found.
problems.interviewTip: Explain why at least one half is sorted when all values are distinct. Check empty and single-element arrays.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation

problems.title: Count Islands in a Binary Grid
problems.statement: Given a rectangular grid of characters '1' (land) and '0' (water), count the number of separate islands. Land cells connect only vertically or horizontally, not diagonally. The method may modify the input grid.

example.explanation: The top-left three land cells form one island; the bottom-right land cell forms another.

problems.approach: Breadth-first search to flood-fill each discovered island
steps: Scan each grid cell row by row. Skip water cells.
When an unvisited land cell is found, increment the island count, mark that cell as water, and enqueue its coordinates.
Process the queue: for each cell, inspect its four neighbors. For every in-bounds land neighbor, mark it as water immediately and enqueue it.
When the queue empties, the whole connected island has been visited. Continue scanning for other land cells.
Return the island count. Marking before enqueueing avoids adding the same cell repeatedly.
problems.interviewTip: Call out that this modifies the grid. If mutation is forbidden, use a separate visited matrix.
problems.source: Original practice problem statement and authored Java implementation
